allPatterns.platform: Page-builder custom widgets (Elementor/WPBakery div "buttons", custom controls with aria-label)
allPatterns.name: div role=button whose accessible name contradicts its visible label
allPatterns.description: A builder renders an interactive control as a <div>/<span> with role="button" (or no role at all) and an aria-label that was authored separately from the visible text — so the on-screen label says "Submit" while the accessible name is "Send form", or the visible text is "Get Quote" but aria-label is "button". Voice-control users saying the visible word can't activate it, and screen-reader users hear something different from what's shown; when role is missing entirely, it isn't even reachable by keyboard.
allPatterns.typicalMarkup:
Submit
Get Quote
allPatterns.whyAutoToolsMiss: When an aria-label is present the control HAS an accessible name, so 4.1.2 "has a name" passes; comparing that name against the visible rendered text to detect a mismatch requires OCR/text extraction of the visible label and a semantic equality judgment that automation doesn't make reliably. (The pure missing-role/not-focusable variant is more linter-catchable.)
allPatterns.realWorldNote: div role=button with aria-label diverging from visible text is the canonical accessible-name-mismatch failure (also a 2.5.3 issue). https://www.makethingsaccessible.com/guides/say-what-you-see-wcag-2-5-3-label-in-name-level-a/ and https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Techniques/failures/F96.html

1.1.1.platform: Spinbutton / number stepper (quantity +/- controls in carts)
1.1.1.name: Stepper +/- buttons with icon-only names and no spinbutton value semantics
1.1.1.description: A quantity stepper has '+' and '−' buttons (often unlabeled icon glyphs) around a value, but the value display is a plain <span> with no role="spinbutton"/aria-valuenow, and the increment/decrement buttons have no accessible name (just a glyph) or a name that does not say what they change. Screen reader users hear 'button button' and an unchanging value when they press them.
1.1.1.typicalMarkup: 1
1.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: If the buttons contain a glyph character (−/+) axe may consider them to have text and pass discernible-text; the '−' may even be read as 'minus' or skipped. Judging that the name does not convey 'decrease quantity' is semantic, and the value <span> not exposing changes (no spinbutton role / live update) is a runtime announcement gap a snapshot scan cannot detect.
1.1.1.realWorldNote: The APG spinbutton pattern requires role=spinbutton with aria-valuenow/min/max and accessible names on the controls; e-commerce quantity steppers commonly ship as glyph-only buttons around a non-semantic value span, a frequent audit finding. https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/spinbutton/

1.1.1.platform: WebAIM Million corpus / Squarespace poster & card image blocks, WordPress media library
1.1.1.name: Alt text is the filename or a generic placeholder
1.1.1.description: An image carries alt text, so the linter sees it as 'present' and passes, but the value is the upload filename (DSC_0042.jpg, hero-banner-final-v2.png), the word 'image', or a stock-photo ID. A screen reader announces 'D S C 0 0 4 2 dot j p g, image' which conveys nothing. Squarespace poster/card/overlap styles silently default alt to the file name when the author leaves it blank, so the markup looks complete while the semantics are useless.
1.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse only test for the PRESENCE of an alt attribute (or a non-empty string). They cannot judge whether the string is meaningful — 'DSC_0042.jpg' is a valid non-empty string. Deciding the alt fails to describe the image, or is redundant filename junk, requires a human to look at the picture and read the text.
1.1.1.realWorldNote: WebAIM Million 2025: missing/poor alt text is the #2 detectable error (18.5% of images, 44% of those on linked images). Squarespace docs confirm poster/card/overlap blocks default alt to the file name when blank: https://support.squarespace.com/hc/en-us/articles/206542357-Adding-alt-text-to-images

1.1.1.platform: WebAIM Million corpus (all builders) — buttons styled as div/span, icon-only controls
1.1.1.name: Empty button / icon control with no accessible name
1.1.1.description: A control is rendered as <div>, <span>, <a>, or an icon font/SVG with no text node and no aria-label, so its accessible name is empty. Screen readers announce 'button' or 'link' with nothing else. Common with hamburger menus, cart/search icons, social-share icons, and 'X' close buttons in page-builder widgets.
1.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: This one IS reliably caught by axe/WAVE ('button-name', 'link-name', 'Empty Button', 'Empty Link') — it is a pure programmatic check for an empty accessible name. Included for completeness as a high-prevalence baseline. Flagged humanJudgmentNeeded=false.
1.1.1.realWorldNote: WebAIM Million 2026: empty buttons on 30.6% of home pages, empty links on 46.3% — both in the top six errors: https://webaim.org/projects/million/

1.1.1.platform: Shopify product pages, WooCommerce variation swatches, custom theme color/size pickers
1.1.1.name: Color-only variant swatches with no text label
1.1.1.description: Product variants are presented as colored squares/circles with no visible or programmatic text. The accessible name is empty or just a hex/SKU, and the selected state is shown only by a border or color change. Screen-reader and colorblind users cannot tell which color is which, nor which is currently selected.
1.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: An empty-name swatch built as a div may trip a name check, but the deeper failures — that COLOR is the only means of conveying the option (1.4.1) and that the SELECTED state is communicated by visual styling alone — require a human to perceive the colors and reason that meaning is lost without them. No linter knows 'navy vs maroon' is the information.
1.1.1.realWorldNote: Shopify's own accessibility best-practices doc warns custom swatches commonly lose keyboard access and text labels: https://shopify.dev/docs/storefronts/themes/best-practices/accessibility . EAA-driven swatch fixes: https://craftshift.com/shopify-european-accessibility-act-swatches/

1.1.1.platform: Banner/promo graphics, pricing tables, infographics rendered as flat images on Wix/Squarespace/Mailchimp landing pages
1.1.1.name: Images of text carrying essential information with no text equivalent
1.1.1.description: Headlines, sale terms, pricing tables, and event details are baked into a single flattened JPG/PNG (often exported from Canva/Figma). The alt text, if any, is a short label that omits the embedded copy, so the actual information (prices, dates, fine print) is unavailable non-visually and pixelates/blurs on zoom.
1.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: No automated tool performs OCR to discover that an image contains essential text, nor that the alt fails to reproduce it. Recognizing 'this picture is really a block of text and the alt drops the price/date' requires a human to read both the image and the alt and compare.
1.1.1.realWorldNote: Images-of-text is a perennial manual-audit and VPAT partial-support item; tied to the alt-text gap WebAIM measures: https://webaim.org/projects/million/2025 . Litigation grounding: the Robles v. Domino's case turned on screen-reader-inaccessible image/graphic content: https://www.boia.org/blog/the-robles-v.-dominos-settlement-and-why-it-matters

1.1.1.platform: Icon-only controls (font-icon or SVG) labelled only via the HTML title attribute (e.g. linked social icons, table action icons)
1.1.1.name: title attribute as the sole accessible name
1.1.1.description: A linked icon or icon button has no text and no aria-label; its only name is a title attribute. title is exposed inconsistently across screen readers (JAWS/NVDA/VoiceOver differ, and it is suppressed when an img alt is present), so the control is effectively unnamed for many users and provides only a flaky mouse-hover tooltip with no keyboard equivalent.
1.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: Per the accname algorithm title IS a valid (last-resort) name source, so axe computes a non-empty accessible name and passes the element. Whether the title is actually announced (and is adequate) depends on the screen reader and on whether better naming was intended; judging the real-world failure needs a human testing with AT.
1.1.1.realWorldNote: 24a11y 'Trials and Tribulations of the Title Attribute'; Silktide 'I thought title text improved accessibility. I was wrong.'; W3C issue 867 on title as sole accName. https://www.24a11y.com/2017/the-trials-and-tribulations-of-the-title-attribute/

1.3.1.platform: Bootstrap / hand-rolled accordion using <a> or <div> headers
1.3.1.name: Accordion header is a non-button with no expanded state
1.3.1.description: Developers copy the accordion visual (a clickable bar that opens a panel) but build the trigger as <a href="#"> or a <div onclick>. Shipping & Returns

1.3.1.platform: Custom <div>/<span> 'button' (icon buttons in CMS widgets, hamburger toggles)
1.3.1.name: Visible label mismatches accessible name on a div-button
1.3.1.description: A control rendered as <div class="btn"> shows the word 'Menu' or a gear icon visually, but its accessible name comes from a stale aria-label like 'button' or 'toggle-1', or from an icon-font ligature that reads as gibberish. 1.3.1.realWorldNote: Harvard HUIT and the freeCodeCamp custom-dropdown guide both document that custom controls whose visible label does not match the accessible name break voice control and confuse screen reader users. https://accessibility.huit.harvard.edu/provide-name-role-and-value-information

1.3.1.platform: Modal dialog (jQuery UI dialog, hand-rolled overlay, many CMS lightboxes)
1.3.1.name: Fake modal: aria-modal set but background not inert and focus not trapped
1.3.1.description: The overlay div carries role="dialog" aria-modal="true" and looks modal, but the developer never traps Tab, never moves initial focus into the dialog, and leaves the background page focusable. Keyboard users Tab straight out of the dialog and onto hidden page content behind the scrim; screen reader users may also reach background content because aria-modal alone does not make content inert.
1.3.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: Static analysis sees correct ARIA: role=dialog + aria-modal=true + accessible name all pass. Whether focus is actually trapped, whether initial focus moves into the dialog, and whether the background is truly inert are runtime keyboard behaviors that require operating the page with Tab/Shift+Tab — axe/WAVE/Lighthouse never press keys.
1.3.1.realWorldNote: MDN and TPGi stress that aria-modal="true" 'does not actually make the element modal — the developer must implement the modal behaviour'; TPGi's modal-accessibility survey found focus management as the most common real failure. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Reference/Attributes/aria-modal and https://www.tpgi.com/the-current-state-of-modal-dialog-accessibility/

1.3.1.description: Tab strips use role="tablist"/role="tab" markup (or just styled links) but every tab is a separate Tab stop and arrow keys do nothing. Users must Tab through all tabs, and roving tabindex (one tabindex=0, rest -1) is absent, breaking the APG keyboard contract. Often aria-selected is also static or missing.

1.3.1.realWorldNote: MDN tab/tablist role docs and Deque's A11y Support Series both specify roving tabindex (active tab tabindex=0, others -1) and arrow-key navigation as the contract that custom tabs routinely omit. https://www.deque.com/blog/a11y-support-series-part-1-aria-tab-panel-accessibility/

1.3.1.platform: Custom toggle switch (settings switches in dashboards, theme togglers)
1.3.1.name: Switch with no role/state and on/off shown by color/position only
1.3.1.description: A pill-shaped toggle is built from two divs; the 'on/off' state is conveyed only by knob position and color. There is no role="switch", no aria-checked, and frequently no accessible name (the visible label is a separate, unassociated div). Screen reader users hear nothing useful and cannot tell if the setting is on or off.
1.3.1.typicalMarkup: Email notifications
1.3.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: If the switch has no role and no name, axe may flag a focusable element with no accessible name in some cases — but many of these get an aria-label and STILL fail because aria-checked is missing or never updates. 1.3.1.realWorldNote: Accessibility Insights 'aria-toggle-field-name', the A11Y Collective, and Atomic A11y checklist all flag missing role=switch / aria-checked / accessible name as the recurring custom-switch defect. https://accessibilityinsights.io/info-examples/web/aria-toggle-field-name/

1.3.1.platform: Menu button + role=menu (app 'kebab' menus, navigation 'mega menus')
1.3.1.name: role=menu misused for site nav; no arrow keys, no haspopup, links not menuitems
1.3.1.description: Developers slap role="menu"/role="menuitem" onto a navigation dropdown of links, or onto an actions menu, but never implement the APG menu keyboard model: no aria-haspopup on the trigger, no focus moved to the first item on open, arrow keys do nothing, Escape does not close. Because role=menu changes how screen readers expose children (links stop being announced as links), the result is worse than plain markup.

The failures are behavioral (missing arrow-key navigation, focus not entering the menu, Escape not closing) plus a semantic judgment that role=menu was the wrong pattern for navigation links — neither is visible in a static DOM scan.
1.3.1.realWorldNote: The Zenyth 'Navigating the Maze of ARIA Menu Roles' guide and APG menubar pattern stress that role=menu is for application menus, demands full arrow-key focus management, and is routinely misapplied to site navigation. https://www.zenythgroup.com/post/navigating-the-maze-of-aria-menu-roles-a-comprehensive-guide

1.3.1.platform: Custom slider (price range filters, noUiSlider clones, hand-rolled drag handles)
1.3.1.name: Slider with no role/value and no keyboard operation
1.3.1.description: A draggable thumb on a track is built from divs with a mousedown handler. There is no role="slider", no aria-valuenow/min/max, no aria-valuetext, and arrow keys do nothing. Screen reader users hear no value and cannot change it; keyboard-only users cannot operate it at all. Dual-thumb range sliders compound this by giving neither thumb a name.
1.3.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: If the thumb has no role and no tabindex, axe sees only inert divs and cannot know they are meant to be a slider, so it raises nothing. Even when role=slider is present, whether arrow keys actually change aria-valuenow is a runtime behavior. The intent ('this draggable thing is a value control') requires visually recognizing the slider, which a linter cannot do.
1.3.1.realWorldNote: TPGi's 'ARIA Slider' series and DigitalA11y's slider-role reference state authors MUST set aria-valuemin/max/now and must update value + aria-valuetext on every arrow/Home/End keypress — the steps custom sliders most often skip. https://www.tpgi.com/aria-slider-part-1/

1.3.1.platform: Carousel / slider (Slick, Swiper defaults, hero banners on CMS themes)
1.3.1.name: Auto-rotating carousel with no pause control and no slide announcement
1.3.1.description: A hero carousel auto-advances every few seconds with no visible/operable pause-stop-hide control. Slides change under keyboard focus, focus is lost when the focused slide rotates away, off-screen slides remain in the tab order and accessibility tree, and slide changes are not exposed via group/aria-roledescription/live region. Vestibular and cognitive users get unstoppable motion; keyboard users get focus thrown to the top of the page.

New In
1.3.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: Auto-rotation, the absence of a pause control, focus loss when slides swap, and links inside hidden slides remaining tabbable are all timing/runtime behaviors. A static scan cannot tell the content is moving or that a pause mechanism is required; deciding whether off-screen slides are correctly hidden needs observing the rotation. WebAIM notes carousels are 'one of the most problematic' widgets precisely for these reasons.
1.3.1.realWorldNote: WebAIM 'Animation and Carousels' and the APG carousel pattern require a pause/stop control, pausing on focus, and hiding non-visible slides; Smashing Magazine's accessible-carousel guide documents the focus-loss-on-rotate bug. https://webaim.org/techniques/carousels/

1.3.1.platform: ARIA tree / file-explorer tree (CMS page-tree pickers, doc nav trees)
1.3.1.name: Tree with Tab-per-node instead of arrow navigation; missing expanded/level
1.3.1.description: A nested expand/collapse tree uses role="tree"/role="treeitem" but is navigated with Tab to every node (instead of a single tab stop + arrow keys), parent nodes lack aria-expanded, end nodes wrongly carry aria-expanded, and aria-level/setsize/posinset are absent on dynamically loaded branches. 1.3.1.platform: alertdialog (confirm/destructive dialogs, 'Are you sure?' modals)
1.3.1.name: Critical confirm dialog uses role=dialog (or none) so it is not announced
1.3.1.description: A 'Delete account — are you sure?' modal is built with role="dialog" (or plain divs) rather than role="alertdialog", and focus is not moved into it. No static linter weighs the urgency of a message.

1.4.1.name: Switch with no role/state and on/off shown by color/position only

1.4.11.platform: Shopify product pages, WooCommerce variation swatches, custom theme color/size pickers
1.4.11.name: Color-only variant swatches with no text label
1.4.11.description: Product variants are presented as colored squares/circles with no visible or programmatic text. The accessible name is empty or just a hex/SKU, and the selected state is shown only by a border or color change. Screen-reader and colorblind users cannot tell which color is which, nor which is currently selected.
1.4.11.whyAutoToolsMiss: An empty-name swatch built as a div may trip a name check, but the deeper failures — that COLOR is the only means of conveying the option (1.4.1) and that the SELECTED state is communicated by visual styling alone — require a human to perceive the colors and reason that meaning is lost without them. No linter knows 'navy vs maroon' is the information.
1.4.11.realWorldNote: Shopify's own accessibility best-practices doc warns custom swatches commonly lose keyboard access and text labels: https://shopify.dev/docs/storefronts/themes/best-practices/accessibility . EAA-driven swatch fixes: https://craftshift.com/shopify-european-accessibility-act-swatches/

1.4.13.platform: Tooltip (title-attribute tooltips, CSS :hover tooltips, icon-info tooltips)
1.4.13.name: Tooltip not dismissible/hoverable/persistent and tied only to hover
1.4.13.description: Help text appears on mouse hover (often via the native title attribute or a CSS :hover-only popup). It disappears the instant the pointer moves, cannot be dismissed with Escape, cannot be hovered to read, and never appears on keyboard focus. Low-vision users who magnify and need to move the pointer onto the tip lose it; keyboard users never see it.
1.4.13.typicalMarkup: ? ?Charged monthly
1.4.13.whyAutoToolsMiss: A title attribute or :hover CSS rule is valid HTML/CSS and triggers no rule. The 1.4.13 requirements (dismissible without moving pointer, hoverable, persistent) are interaction qualities that can only be evaluated by hovering, pressing Escape, and trying to move onto the popup — automated tools do not exercise hover/focus interaction states.
1.4.13.realWorldNote: Sarah Higley's 'Tooltips in the time of WCAG 2.1' and W3C Understanding 1.4.13 list 'content shown on hover not hoverable' and 'not dismissible without moving the pointer' as the canonical failures; W3C also flags relying on the title attribute. https://sarahmhigley.com/writing/tooltips-in-wcag-21/

2.1.1.platform: Tabs widget (Bootstrap nav-tabs, hand-rolled tab UIs)
2.1.1.name: Tabs with no roving tabindex / no arrow-key support
2.1.1.description: Tab strips use role="tablist"/role="tab" markup (or just styled links) but every tab is a separate Tab stop and arrow keys do nothing. Users must Tab through all tabs, and roving tabindex (one tabindex=0, rest -1) is absent, breaking the APG keyboard contract. Often aria-selected is also static or missing.
2.1.1.typicalMarkup:
• Overview
  • Specs
  • Reviews
2.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: axe has a 'tablist must contain tabs' structural check but does not verify the roving-tabindex pattern or arrow-key handling — those are runtime keyboard behaviors. A page where every tab is independently Tab-focusable is technically operable, so it does not fail any static rule; the broken expectation (arrow keys move between tabs) is only observable by operating it.
2.1.1.realWorldNote: MDN tab/tablist role docs and Deque's A11y Support Series both specify roving tabindex (active tab tabindex=0, others -1) and arrow-key navigation as the contract that custom tabs routinely omit. https://www.deque.com/blog/a11y-support-series-part-1-aria-tab-panel-accessibility/

2.1.1.platform: Menu button + role=menu (app 'kebab' menus, navigation 'mega menus')
2.1.1.name: role=menu misused for site nav; no arrow keys, no haspopup, links not menuitems
2.1.1.description: Developers slap role="menu"/role="menuitem" onto a navigation dropdown of links, or onto an actions menu, but never implement the APG menu keyboard model: no aria-haspopup on the trigger, no focus moved to the first item on open, arrow keys do nothing, Escape does not close. Because role=menu changes how screen readers expose children (links stop being announced as links), the result is worse than plain markup.
2.1.1.typicalMarkup:
• Profile
  • Log out
2.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: The ARIA is syntactically valid (menu contains menuitems), so structural rules pass. The failures are behavioral (missing arrow-key navigation, focus not entering the menu, Escape not closing) plus a semantic judgment that role=menu was the wrong pattern for navigation links — neither is visible in a static DOM scan.
2.1.1.realWorldNote: The Zenyth 'Navigating the Maze of ARIA Menu Roles' guide and APG menubar pattern stress that role=menu is for application menus, demands full arrow-key focus management, and is routinely misapplied to site navigation. https://www.zenythgroup.com/post/navigating-the-maze-of-aria-menu-roles-a-comprehensive-guide

2.1.1.platform: Custom slider (price range filters, noUiSlider clones, hand-rolled drag handles)
2.1.1.name: Slider with no role/value and no keyboard operation
2.1.1.description: A draggable thumb on a track is built from divs with a mousedown handler. There is no role="slider", no aria-valuenow/min/max, no aria-valuetext, and arrow keys do nothing. Screen reader users hear no value and cannot change it; keyboard-only users cannot operate it at all. Dual-thumb range sliders compound this by giving neither thumb a name.
2.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: If the thumb has no role and no tabindex, axe sees only inert divs and cannot know they are meant to be a slider, so it raises nothing. Even when role=slider is present, whether arrow keys actually change aria-valuenow is a runtime behavior. The intent ('this draggable thing is a value control') requires visually recognizing the slider, which a linter cannot do.
2.1.1.realWorldNote: TPGi's 'ARIA Slider' series and DigitalA11y's slider-role reference state authors MUST set aria-valuemin/max/now and must update value + aria-valuetext on every arrow/Home/End keypress — the steps custom sliders most often skip. https://www.tpgi.com/aria-slider-part-1/

2.1.1.platform: Carousel / slider (Slick, Swiper defaults, hero banners on CMS themes)
2.1.1.name: Auto-rotating carousel with no pause control and no slide announcement
2.1.1.description: A hero carousel auto-advances every few seconds with no visible/operable pause-stop-hide control. Slides change under keyboard focus, focus is lost when the focused slide rotates away, off-screen slides remain in the tab order and accessibility tree, and slide changes are not exposed via group/aria-roledescription/live region. Vestibular and cognitive users get unstoppable motion; keyboard users get focus thrown to the top of the page.
2.1.1.typicalMarkup:
Big Sale
New In
2.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: Auto-rotation, the absence of a pause control, focus loss when slides swap, and links inside hidden slides remaining tabbable are all timing/runtime behaviors. A static scan cannot tell the content is moving or that a pause mechanism is required; deciding whether off-screen slides are correctly hidden needs observing the rotation. WebAIM notes carousels are 'one of the most problematic' widgets precisely for these reasons.
2.1.1.realWorldNote: WebAIM 'Animation and Carousels' and the APG carousel pattern require a pause/stop control, pausing on focus, and hiding non-visible slides; Smashing Magazine's accessible-carousel guide documents the focus-loss-on-rotate bug. https://webaim.org/techniques/carousels/

2.1.1.platform: ARIA tree / file-explorer tree (CMS page-tree pickers, doc nav trees)
2.1.1.name: Tree with Tab-per-node instead of arrow navigation; missing expanded/level
2.1.1.description: A nested expand/collapse tree uses role="tree"/role="treeitem" but is navigated with Tab to every node (instead of a single tab stop + arrow keys), parent nodes lack aria-expanded, end nodes wrongly carry aria-expanded, and aria-level/setsize/posinset are absent on dynamically loaded branches. Screen reader users get no hierarchy or open/closed state; the keyboard model contradicts the APG tree contract.
2.1.1.typicalMarkup:
• Docs
    • Intro
2.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: The role nesting (tree > treeitem > group) is structurally valid so static checks pass. Whether arrow keys navigate, whether the tree is a single tab stop, and whether aria-expanded toggles on expand/collapse are runtime behaviors. Knowing aria-expanded is missing on a parent requires knowing which nodes have children at runtime — invisible to a snapshot scan.
2.1.1.realWorldNote: MDN tree/treeitem role docs and Accessible Culture's '(Not so) Simple ARIA Tree Views' document that trees use arrow-key navigation (not Tab), require aria-expanded only on parents, and need aria-level/setsize/posinset on dynamic nodes — all routinely botched. https://accessibleculture.org/articles/2013/02/not-so-simple-aria-tree-views-and-screen-readers/

2.1.1.platform: Radio group (custom styled radios, form-builder widgets, Shoelace-style components)
2.1.1.name: Custom radios: no grouping, every radio a tab stop, no arrow selection
2.1.1.description: Styled radio buttons are built from divs (or are native radios stripped of fieldset/legend and group semantics). There is no role="radiogroup" or fieldset/legend, so the question text is never associated; each radio is a separate Tab stop instead of one stop with arrow-key selection; and the group label is unannounced. Screen reader users hear isolated options with no context or count.
2.1.1.typicalMarkup:
Choose a plan

Basic
Pro
2.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss:
Individual role=radio elements with text content pass name/role checks. The missing radiogroup association (the 'Choose a plan' label is a sibling

, not a programmatic group name) and the broken single-tab-stop + arrow-key model are a structural-relationship judgment and a runtime behavior respectively — TestParty reports 95% of sites have at least one improperly grouped radio set that scanners do not catch as a hard failure.
2.1.1.realWorldNote: TestParty's radio-group remediation writeup and shoelace-style/shoelace issue #218 document ungrouped radios and Tab-per-radio (instead of arrow navigation) as pervasive custom-component failures. https://testparty.ai/blog/accessible-radio-groups-html-fast-remediation-large-sites and https://github.com/shoelace-style/shoelace/issues/218

2.1.1.name: Custom listbox: options not announced, selection state visual-only
2.1.1.description: A fake select shows a styled options panel of <li> items. The trigger lacks combobox/button semantics with aria-expanded, the panel is not role="listbox" with role="option" children, selection is shown only by a checkmark/highlight (no aria-selected), and focus/active option is not tracked. Screen reader users cannot tell which option is selected or how many exist; keyboard arrow navigation through options is often missing.
2.1.1.typicalMarkup:
United States
  • United States
  • Canada
2.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: The trigger div has an accessible name and the list is a valid <ul>, so static checks pass. That selection is conveyed only by a CSS class/checkmark (no aria-selected — a use-of-color/visual-only-state issue) and that arrow-key navigation is absent are visual and runtime judgments. The freeCodeCamp and Chris Henrick writeups stress native <select> is far safer precisely because these get botched.
2.1.1.realWorldNote: freeCodeCamp's accessible custom-dropdown guide and Chris Henrick's 'Custom and Accessible Select Menus Aren't Easy' document missing role=listbox/option, missing aria-selected, and absent keyboard support as the standard custom-listbox failures. https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/how-to-build-an-accessible-custom-dropdown-select-element/

2.1.1.platform: WordPress slider plugins (Slider Revolution, Smart Slider), Elementor/Divi carousels, Wix Pro Gallery
2.1.1.name: Auto-rotating carousel, keyboard-inaccessible, no pause
2.1.1.description: A hero carousel auto-advances on a timer with no pause/stop control, prev/next arrows are non-focusable divs, and slide changes are not announced. Keyboard users cannot reach controls; the moving content steals reading position; offscreen slides may still be in the tab order as hidden focusable links.
2.1.1.typicalMarkup: Shop the sale
2.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: Auto-rotation timing and the absence of a pause control are temporal/behavioral and not in the static DOM signature. Tools may catch a div with onclick lacking a role, but cannot verify keyboard reachability of the rotation, that focus is trapped/lost between slides, or that offscreen slides leak into the tab order — all need manual keyboard testing.
2.1.1.realWorldNote: WCAG-ART and the A11Y Collective document carousel pause/keyboard/announce failures as classic manual-test items: https://www.a11y-collective.com/blog/accessible-carousel/ ; WP slider accessibility caveats: https://www.abrightclearweb.com/accessible-slider-wordpress/

2.1.1.platform: Bootstrap/template tabs, accordions, and custom dropdowns in CMS themes
2.1.1.name: Custom widget role present but state/keyboard support missing
2.1.1.description: A theme implements tabs/accordions/menus with role=tab/button and ARIA, satisfying role checks, but the dynamic VALUE/STATE is wrong or static: aria-expanded never toggles, aria-selected is hard-coded, the panel relationship (aria-controls) is broken, and arrow-key navigation is absent. ARIA presence makes the page LOOK accessible while behaving inaccessibly.
2.1.1.typicalMarkup:
<button aria-expanded="false" class="accordion">Shipping</button>
<!-- clicking opens the panel visually but aria-expanded stays "false"; no arrow-key support -->
2.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: Static scans confirm the ATTRIBUTES exist and are valid; they cannot verify the attribute VALUE tracks the live UI state (aria-expanded staying false after opening) or that keyboard interaction patterns work — these are dynamic, requiring activation and re-inspection. This is precisely why WebAIM finds MORE detected errors on ARIA-heavy pages.
2.1.1.realWorldNote: WebAIM Million: pages WITH ARIA average ~34-69% MORE detected errors than pages without — broken/incomplete ARIA is a leading cause: https://webaim.org/projects/million/2024 ; 2026 confirms the pattern: https://webaim.org/projects/million/

2.1.1.platform: Marketing-site / CMS clickable cards and tiles built as div/span with onclick (Webflow interactions, custom hero tiles, jQuery .click handlers)
2.1.1.name: div/span with click handler as a fake button (no role, no keyboard)
2.1.1.description: An interactive control is a bare div or span with a JS click handler, no role, no tabindex, and only an onclick (no keydown). Keyboard users cannot reach or activate it, and screen readers announce nothing meaningful. This is the canonical W3C F59 failure.
2.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: Partially auto-detectable (axe 'interactive controls must be operable' / clickable element flags exist), but tools frequently miss it when the handler is attached via addEventListener at runtime rather than an inline onclick attribute, or delegated from a parent. Confirming it is genuinely interactive (vs. a decorative animated div) often needs a human to click/Tab and observe.
2.1.1.realWorldNote: W3C failure F59 (script makes div/span a UI control without a role); Deque 'Building Accessible Buttons with ARIA'. https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG20-TECHS/F59.html

2.1.1.platform: Modal dialogs, off-canvas drawers, and carousels (Bootstrap modal backdrops, slick/swiper slides, third-party overlay libs) that set aria-hidden on containers holding focusable elements
2.1.1.name: aria-hidden="true" on (or wrapping) focusable elements
2.1.1.description: A container is hidden from AT with aria-hidden="true" but still contains tabbable controls (links, buttons, inputs) that were not made inert / tabindex=-1. Keyboard users can Tab into a control the screen reader refuses to announce — 'focus goes nowhere' — producing a phantom/ghost focus and broken navigation. Common on inactive carousel slides and behind-modal page content.
2.1.1.typicalMarkup: Buy now
2.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: Mostly auto-detectable (axe rule 'aria-hidden elements do not contain focusable elements'). Included for completeness. Tools can miss it when focusability comes from runtime-added tabindex, or when the aria-hidden is toggled on only in a state (modal open) the scanner never enters; reaching that state is a human/dynamic step.
2.1.1.realWorldNote: GetWCAG 4.1.2 fix guide 'avoid focusable elements inside aria-hidden containers'; ACT rules issue 643; UW accessibility 'aria-hidden elements'. https://getwcag.com/en/accessibility-guide/aria-hidden-focus

2.1.1.platform: Page-builder custom widgets (Elementor/WPBakery div "buttons", custom controls with aria-label)
2.1.1.name: div role=button whose accessible name contradicts its visible label
2.1.1.description: A builder renders an interactive control as a <div>/<span> with role="button" (or no role at all) and an aria-label that was authored separately from the visible text — so the on-screen label says "Submit" while the accessible name is "Send form", or the visible text is "Get Quote" but aria-label is "button". Voice-control users saying the visible word can't activate it, and screen-reader users hear something different from what's shown; when role is missing entirely, it isn't even reachable by keyboard.
2.1.1.typicalMarkup:
Submit
Get Quote
2.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: When an aria-label is present the control HAS an accessible name, so 4.1.2 "has a name" passes; comparing that name against the visible rendered text to detect a mismatch requires OCR/text extraction of the visible label and a semantic equality judgment that automation doesn't make reliably. (The pure missing-role/not-focusable variant is more linter-catchable.)
2.1.1.realWorldNote: div role=button with aria-label diverging from visible text is the canonical accessible-name-mismatch failure (also a 2.5.3 issue). https://www.makethingsaccessible.com/guides/say-what-you-see-wcag-2-5-3-label-in-name-level-a/ and https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Techniques/failures/F96.html

2.1.2.platform: Modal dialog (jQuery UI dialog, hand-rolled overlay, many CMS lightboxes)
2.1.2.name: Fake modal: aria-modal set but background not inert and focus not trapped
2.1.2.description: The overlay div carries role="dialog" aria-modal="true" and looks modal, but the developer never traps Tab, never moves initial focus into the dialog, and leaves the background page focusable. Keyboard users Tab straight out of the dialog and onto hidden page content behind the scrim; screen reader users may also reach background content because aria-modal alone does not make content inert.
2.1.2.whyAutoToolsMiss: Static analysis sees correct ARIA: role=dialog + aria-modal=true + accessible name all pass. Whether focus is actually trapped, whether initial focus moves into the dialog, and whether the background is truly inert are runtime keyboard behaviors that require operating the page with Tab/Shift+Tab — axe/WAVE/Lighthouse never press keys.
2.1.2.realWorldNote: MDN and TPGi stress that aria-modal="true" 'does not actually make the element modal — the developer must implement the modal behaviour'; TPGi's modal-accessibility survey found focus management as the most common real failure. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Reference/Attributes/aria-modal and https://www.tpgi.com/the-current-state-of-modal-dialog-accessibility/

2.1.2.platform: accessiBe / UserWay / AudioEye overlay widgets injected over any CMS
2.1.2.name: Overlay-injected accessible names that mismatch the visible control
2.1.2.description: An automated accessibility-overlay 'fixes' controls by injecting aria-labels guessed from nearby text, icons, or filenames. The injected name frequently does not match the control's visible label or function (a 'Search' field labeled 'button', a close 'X' labeled 'menu'), so the accessible name and visible label diverge — and the widget can also trap screen-reader focus after its own dialog closes.
2.1.2.typicalMarkup:
<!-- overlay rewrites this -->
<button aria-label="link 2">Contact Us</button>
<input type="search" aria-label="submit" placeholder="Search...">
2.1.2.whyAutoToolsMiss: Both the overlay's injected name and the visible label are syntactically valid, so a linter sees an accessible name present and passes. Detecting that the programmatic NAME contradicts the VISIBLE label (and that voice-control users can no longer say the label) requires comparing rendered text against the computed name — a human semantic comparison. Tools that scan post-overlay DOM are actively fooled.
2.1.2.realWorldNote: FTC fined accessiBe $1M for misleading claims; 800+ overlay users still sued in 2023-24. Adrian Roselli's tracking: https://adrianroselli.com/2020/06/accessibe-will-get-you-sued.html ; FTC: https://techcrunch.com/2025/01/03/ftc-orders-ai-accessibility-startup-accessibe-to-pay-1m-for-misleading-advertising

2.1.2.platform: Cookie-consent banners, newsletter modals, promo pop-ups (OneTrust, Privy, Mailchimp, Wix popups)
2.1.2.name: Modal/pop-up keyboard trap or focus-not-managed
2.1.2.description: A modal or interstitial appears but focus is not moved into it, focus is not trapped within it (so keyboard users tab to the obscured page behind), or — the inverse failure — focus IS trapped with no keyboard-reachable close, stranding the user. The page behind also remains in the tab order under the overlay.
2.1.2.whyAutoToolsMiss: Focus behavior is dynamic and only observable by actually tabbing through after the modal opens. A static scan sees a div with some content; it cannot detect that focus was never moved in, that the user can tab behind the overlay, or that there is no keyboard escape (2.1.2). Requires manual keyboard testing.
2.1.2.realWorldNote: The Murphy v. Eyebobs overlay case specifically cited a promo pop-up and a modal dialog that were not keyboard/screen-reader accessible: https://www.accessibility.works/blog/avoid-accessibility-overlay-tools-toolbar-plugins/ ; modal focus-trap failures are a top serial-plaintiff demand-letter item.

2.4.2.platform: Single-page app (React Router, Vue Router, Angular) route transitions
2.4.2.name: <title> and focus never update on client-side route change
2.4.2.description: Navigating between SPA 'pages' swaps the DOM without a reload, but document.title is left at the template default ('My App') for every route, focus stays on the clicked link or the top of the old view, and no live region announces the new page. Screen reader users have no idea they navigated or where they are; the page title — a primary orientation cue — is identical or stale across routes.
2.4.2.typicalMarkup:
<title>My App</title>
<!-- user clicks 'Checkout'; URL becomes /checkout; main content swaps -->
<!-- <title> still 'My App'; focus still on the clicked nav link; no aria-live announcement -->
2.4.2.whyAutoToolsMiss: A single-snapshot scan sees one <title> that is present and non-empty, so 2.4.2 passes. The defect is that the title is the SAME (or unchanged) across multiple distinct views — only visible by navigating between routes and comparing, plus judging that the title no longer describes the content. Automated tools audit one URL state, not transitions.
2.4.2.realWorldNote: Hidde de Vries, Kitty Giraudel, and Deque all document SPA route changes leaving document.title stale and focus unmanaged as a flagship screen-reader failure of frameworks. https://hidde.blog/accessible-page-titles-in-a-single-page-app/ and https://www.deque.com/blog/accessibility-tips-in-single-page-applications/

2.4.2.platform: React/Vue/Angular SPAs built on Next.js, Gatsby, Shopify Hydrogen, headless storefronts
2.4.2.name: SPA <title> and focus never update on client-side route change
2.4.2.description: Navigating between client-rendered views swaps the main content but never updates document.title and never moves focus, so the page title is frozen at the initial route ('Home') and the screen reader is left on a now-detached element. The user has no confirmation a navigation happened or where they landed.
2.4.2.typicalMarkup:
<!-- title stuck on first load across every route -->
<title>Acme Store - Home</title>
<!-- /products, /cart, /checkout all render under this same title; no focus move, no live-region announce -->
2.4.2.whyAutoToolsMiss: A single-snapshot scan sees a valid, non-empty <title> and passes 2.4.2. The failure is DYNAMIC and BEHAVIORAL — it only manifests across a route transition, which axe/Lighthouse (point-in-time DOM scans) never exercise. Catching it requires interacting (clicking a nav link) and observing that title/focus did not change.
2.4.2.realWorldNote: Documented SPA failure mode; Kitty Giraudel and Deque both cover the fix (update title + manage focus/live region on route change): https://kittygiraudel.com/2020/01/15/accessible-title-in-a-single-page-react-application/ , https://www.deque.com/blog/accessibility-tips-in-single-page-applications/

2.4.2.platform: Site templates / themes where the boilerplate <title> was never customized
2.4.2.name: Template-default page title left unchanged
2.4.2.description: Pages ship with the theme's placeholder title — 'Home', 'Untitled', 'My WordPress Blog', 'Page Title', or the same site name on every URL. The <title> exists and is non-empty (so 2.4.2 passes mechanically) but does not describe the page's topic or purpose, defeating tab/window/history orientation and search.
2.4.2.whyAutoToolsMiss: axe/WAVE only verify a <title> exists and is non-empty; 'Home' and 'Untitled' satisfy that. Judging that the title is a leftover template default, generic, or duplicated across pages so it fails to DESCRIBE the page requires understanding what the page is actually about — human judgment.
2.4.2.realWorldNote: Recurring VPAT 'partial support' note and a staple manual-audit finding; WebAIM lists document title quality as a manual check beyond the automated presence test: https://webaim.org/projects/million/ (document-title issues are tracked separately from automated error counts).

2.4.2.platform: Single-page apps (React Router / Vue Router / Angular routing in SPA themes and dashboards) where document.title is not updated on route change
2.4.2.name: SPA <title> never updates on client-side route change
2.4.2.description: Navigating between client-side routes swaps the view but leaves <title> at the initial app shell value (e.g. 'My App'). Screen-reader users get no title announcement on 'navigation', browser tabs/history/bookmarks all read the same generic title, and there is no programmatic signal that the page changed.
2.4.2.whyAutoToolsMiss: A single-page scan finds a valid, non-empty <title>, so 2.4.2 passes. The defect only manifests across route transitions — the scanner would have to drive the SPA, change routes, and compare titles. Judging whether each route's title is unique and descriptive is also a contextual call.
2.4.2.realWorldNote: Widely documented SPA a11y gap (gov.uk / Marcy Sutton / TPGI guidance on managing focus and document.title on route change in React/Vue/Angular SPAs).

2.4.2.platform: React / Vue / Angular SPA with client-side router (React Router, Vue Router)
2.4.2.name: <title> and focus never update on route change
2.4.2.description: Client-side navigation swaps the view in place without a full page load. document.title stays at the app's default, and focus remains wherever the user clicked, so screen-reader users hear no page-change announcement and keyboard users are stranded mid-page. The browser history changes but AT perceives nothing — the user has no idea they navigated or where they are.
2.4.2.typicalMarkup:
<!-- after navigating /home -> /checkout, title is unchanged -->
<head><title>My App</title></head>
<!-- new view rendered; no focus move, no title update -->
2.4.2.whyAutoToolsMiss: A single-snapshot scan of any one route finds a present, non-empty <title>, so 2.4.2 passes per page. The failure is the absence of an update across a runtime navigation event — automation auditing one DOM state cannot observe that the title/focus failed to change on transition.
2.4.2.realWorldNote: Widely documented SPA failure mode; routers don't reset focus or title on navigation. https://kittygiraudel.com/2020/01/15/accessible-title-in-a-single-page-react-application/ and https://github.com/remix-run/react-router/discussions/9863

2.4.3.platform: Modal dialog (jQuery UI dialog, hand-rolled overlay, many CMS lightboxes)
2.4.3.name: Fake modal: aria-modal set but background not inert and focus not trapped
2.4.3.description: The overlay div carries role="dialog" aria-modal="true" and looks modal, but the developer never traps Tab, never moves initial focus into the dialog, and leaves the background page focusable. Keyboard users Tab straight out of the dialog and onto hidden page content behind the scrim; screen reader users may also reach background content because aria-modal alone does not make content inert.
2.4.3.whyAutoToolsMiss: Static analysis sees correct ARIA: role=dialog + aria-modal=true + accessible name all pass. Whether focus is actually trapped, whether initial focus moves into the dialog, and whether the background is truly inert are runtime keyboard behaviors that require operating the page with Tab/Shift+Tab — axe/WAVE/Lighthouse never press keys.
2.4.3.realWorldNote: MDN and TPGi stress that aria-modal="true" 'does not actually make the element modal — the developer must implement the modal behaviour'; TPGi's modal-accessibility survey found focus management as the most common real failure. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Reference/Attributes/aria-modal and https://www.tpgi.com/the-current-state-of-modal-dialog-accessibility/

2.4.3.platform: Single-page app (React Router, Vue Router, Angular) route transitions
2.4.3.name: <title> and focus never update on client-side route change
2.4.3.description: Navigating between SPA 'pages' swaps the DOM without a reload, but document.title is left at the template default ('My App') for every route, focus stays on the clicked link or the top of the old view, and no live region announces the new page. Screen reader users have no idea they navigated or where they are; the page title — a primary orientation cue — is identical or stale across routes.
2.4.3.typicalMarkup:
<title>My App</title>
<!-- user clicks 'Checkout'; URL becomes /checkout; main content swaps -->
<!-- <title> still 'My App'; focus still on the clicked nav link; no aria-live announcement -->
2.4.3.whyAutoToolsMiss: A single-snapshot scan sees one <title> that is present and non-empty, so 2.4.2 passes. The defect is that the title is the SAME (or unchanged) across multiple distinct views — only visible by navigating between routes and comparing, plus judging that the title no longer describes the content. Automated tools audit one URL state, not transitions.
2.4.3.realWorldNote: Hidde de Vries, Kitty Giraudel, and Deque all document SPA route changes leaving document.title stale and focus unmanaged as a flagship screen-reader failure of frameworks. https://hidde.blog/accessible-page-titles-in-a-single-page-app/ and https://www.deque.com/blog/accessibility-tips-in-single-page-applications/

2.4.3.platform: Carousel / slider (Slick, Swiper defaults, hero banners on CMS themes)
2.4.3.name: Auto-rotating carousel with no pause control and no slide announcement
2.4.3.description: A hero carousel auto-advances every few seconds with no visible/operable pause-stop-hide control. Slides change under keyboard focus, focus is lost when the focused slide rotates away, off-screen slides remain in the tab order and accessibility tree, and slide changes are not exposed via group/aria-roledescription/live region. Vestibular and cognitive users get unstoppable motion; keyboard users get focus thrown to the top of the page.
2.4.3.typicalMarkup:
Big Sale
New In
2.4.3.whyAutoToolsMiss: Auto-rotation, the absence of a pause control, focus loss when slides swap, and links inside hidden slides remaining tabbable are all timing/runtime behaviors. A static scan cannot tell the content is moving or that a pause mechanism is required; deciding whether off-screen slides are correctly hidden needs observing the rotation. WebAIM notes carousels are 'one of the most problematic' widgets precisely for these reasons.
2.4.3.realWorldNote: WebAIM 'Animation and Carousels' and the APG carousel pattern require a pause/stop control, pausing on focus, and hiding non-visible slides; Smashing Magazine's accessible-carousel guide documents the focus-loss-on-rotate bug. https://webaim.org/techniques/carousels/

2.4.3.name: Critical confirm dialog uses role=dialog (or none) so it is not announced
2.4.3.description: A 'Delete account — are you sure?' modal is built with role="dialog" (or plain divs) rather than role="alertdialog", and focus is not moved into it. The urgent message is not announced as an alert, focus stays behind it, and a screen reader user may confirm a destructive action without ever hearing the warning.
2.4.3.typicalMarkup: Delete your account? This cannot be undone.
2.4.3.whyAutoToolsMiss: role=dialog is valid ARIA, so no rule fails. Whether the dialog SHOULD be an alertdialog (because it carries an urgent, action-blocking message) is a semantic/contextual judgment about the content's importance; whether focus moves into it and the alert is announced are runtime behaviors. No static linter weighs the urgency of a message.
2.4.3.realWorldNote: APG distinguishes alertdialog (interrupts with an important message requiring a response) from dialog; MDN dialog-role docs note focus must move into the dialog — both are commonly skipped on confirm/destructive modals. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Reference/Roles/dialog_role

2.4.3.platform: React/Vue/Angular SPAs built on Next.js, Gatsby, Shopify Hydrogen, headless storefronts
2.4.3.name: SPA <title> and focus never update on client-side route change
2.4.3.description: Navigating between client-rendered views swaps the main content but never updates document.title and never moves focus, so the page title is frozen at the initial route ('Home') and the screen reader is left on a now-detached element. The user has no confirmation a navigation happened or where they landed.
2.4.3.typicalMarkup:
<!-- title stuck on first load across every route -->
<title>Acme Store - Home</title>
<!-- /products, /cart, /checkout all render under this same title; no focus move, no live-region announce -->
2.4.3.whyAutoToolsMiss: A single-snapshot scan sees a valid, non-empty <title> and passes 2.4.2. The failure is DYNAMIC and BEHAVIORAL — it only manifests across a route transition, which axe/Lighthouse (point-in-time DOM scans) never exercise. Catching it requires interacting (clicking a nav link) and observing that title/focus did not change.
2.4.3.realWorldNote: Documented SPA failure mode; Kitty Giraudel and Deque both cover the fix (update title + manage focus/live region on route change): https://kittygiraudel.com/2020/01/15/accessible-title-in-a-single-page-react-application/ , https://www.deque.com/blog/accessibility-tips-in-single-page-applications/

2.4.3.platform: WordPress slider plugins (Slider Revolution, Smart Slider), Elementor/Divi carousels, Wix Pro Gallery
2.4.3.name: Auto-rotating carousel, keyboard-inaccessible, no pause
2.4.3.description: A hero carousel auto-advances on a timer with no pause/stop control, prev/next arrows are non-focusable divs, and slide changes are not announced. Keyboard users cannot reach controls; the moving content steals reading position; offscreen slides may still be in the tab order as hidden focusable links.
2.4.3.typicalMarkup: Shop the sale
2.4.3.whyAutoToolsMiss: Auto-rotation timing and the absence of a pause control are temporal/behavioral and not in the static DOM signature. Tools may catch a div with onclick lacking a role, but cannot verify keyboard reachability of the rotation, that focus is trapped/lost between slides, or that offscreen slides leak into the tab order — all need manual keyboard testing.
2.4.3.realWorldNote: WCAG-ART and the A11Y Collective document carousel pause/keyboard/announce failures as classic manual-test items: https://www.a11y-collective.com/blog/accessible-carousel/ ; WP slider accessibility caveats: https://www.abrightclearweb.com/accessible-slider-wordpress/

2.4.3.platform: Cookie-consent banners, newsletter modals, promo pop-ups (OneTrust, Privy, Mailchimp, Wix popups)
2.4.3.name: Modal/pop-up keyboard trap or focus-not-managed
2.4.3.description: A modal or interstitial appears but focus is not moved into it, focus is not trapped within it (so keyboard users tab to the obscured page behind), or — the inverse failure — focus IS trapped with no keyboard-reachable close, stranding the user. The page behind also remains in the tab order under the overlay.
2.4.3.whyAutoToolsMiss: Focus behavior is dynamic and only observable by actually tabbing through after the modal opens. A static scan sees a div with some content; it cannot detect that focus was never moved in, that the user can tab behind the overlay, or that there is no keyboard escape (2.1.2). Requires manual keyboard testing.
2.4.3.realWorldNote: The Murphy v. Eyebobs overlay case specifically cited a promo pop-up and a modal dialog that were not keyboard/screen-reader accessible: https://www.accessibility.works/blog/avoid-accessibility-overlay-tools-toolbar-plugins/ ; modal focus-trap failures are a top serial-plaintiff demand-letter item.

2.4.3.platform: Modal dialogs, off-canvas drawers, and carousels (Bootstrap modal backdrops, slick/swiper slides, third-party overlay libs) that set aria-hidden on containers holding focusable elements
2.4.3.name: aria-hidden="true" on (or wrapping) focusable elements
2.4.3.description: A container is hidden from AT with aria-hidden="true" but still contains tabbable controls (links, buttons, inputs) that were not made inert / tabindex=-1. Keyboard users can Tab into a control the screen reader refuses to announce — 'focus goes nowhere' — producing a phantom/ghost focus and broken navigation. Common on inactive carousel slides and behind-modal page content.
2.4.3.typicalMarkup: Buy now
2.4.3.whyAutoToolsMiss: Mostly auto-detectable (axe rule 'aria-hidden elements do not contain focusable elements'). Included for completeness. Tools can miss it when focusability comes from runtime-added tabindex, or when the aria-hidden is toggled on only in a state (modal open) the scanner never enters; reaching that state is a human/dynamic step.
2.4.3.realWorldNote: GetWCAG 4.1.2 fix guide 'avoid focusable elements inside aria-hidden containers'; ACT rules issue 643; UW accessibility 'aria-hidden elements'. https://getwcag.com/en/accessibility-guide/aria-hidden-focus

2.4.3.platform: React / Vue / Angular SPA with client-side router (React Router, Vue Router)
2.4.3.name: <title> and focus never update on route change
2.4.3.description: Client-side navigation swaps the view in place without a full page load. document.title stays at the app's default, and focus remains wherever the user clicked, so screen-reader users hear no page-change announcement and keyboard users are stranded mid-page. The browser history changes but AT perceives nothing — the user has no idea they navigated or where they are.
2.4.3.typicalMarkup:
<!-- after navigating /home -> /checkout, title is unchanged -->
<head><title>My App</title></head>
<!-- new view rendered; no focus move, no title update -->
2.4.3.whyAutoToolsMiss: A single-snapshot scan of any one route finds a present, non-empty <title>, so 2.4.2 passes per page. The failure is the absence of an update across a runtime navigation event — automation auditing one DOM state cannot observe that the title/focus failed to change on transition.
2.4.3.realWorldNote: Widely documented SPA failure mode; routers don't reset focus or title on navigation. https://kittygiraudel.com/2020/01/15/accessible-title-in-a-single-page-react-application/ and https://github.com/remix-run/react-router/discussions/9863

2.4.3.platform: Page builders using CSS flexbox/grid order (Elementor, Webflow, Bricks, custom responsive layouts)
2.4.3.name: Visual reorder via CSS order/row-reverse desyncs DOM/focus order
2.4.3.description: Designers rearrange columns/cards visually with flex order, order: -1, flex-direction: row-reverse, or grid placement while leaving DOM order untouched. The page looks correct, but keyboard Tab order and screen-reader reading order follow the (now-stale) DOM, so focus jumps erratically across the page and content is read in a sequence that doesn't match the visual layout. Especially common at the responsive breakpoint where source order was authored for desktop.
2.4.3.whyAutoToolsMiss: DOM and focus order are technically valid and tools don't compute the rendered visual geometry to compare against tab sequence. Deciding that the visual order is meaningful (a sequence of steps) and therefore must match DOM order requires understanding content meaning and seeing the rendered layout.
2.4.3.realWorldNote: Classic Flexbox/Grid reorder pitfall affecting 1.3.2 and 2.4.3. https://wcag.dock.codes/documentation/wcag132/ and https://testparty.ai/blog/wcag-2-4-3-focus-order-2025-guide

2.4.3.platform: PDF-to-HTML export tools (Acrobat "Export as HTML", InDesign publish, pdf2htmlEX preserved-layout mode)
2.4.3.name: Absolutely-positioned spans replace semantic structure
2.4.3.description: "Preserved layout" conversion reproduces the PDF pixel-for-pixel by emitting hundreds of absolutely-positioned <span>/<div> elements, one per text run, with no headings, lists, or paragraphs — and DOM order driven by the PDF's internal object order, not reading order. Visually identical to the source, but linearized AT output is scrambled: column text interleaves, headings are plain spans, and there is no navigable structure.
2.4.3.whyAutoToolsMiss: Markup is valid; there are no missing alts or empty headings to flag. Tools don't reconstruct visual reading flow from absolute coordinates to detect that the DOM sequence diverges from the visual sequence, nor that prominent spans are functioning as headings. Reading order correctness and implied structure are human judgments.
2.4.3.realWorldNote: Preserved-layout PDF-to-HTML uses absolutely-positioned spans that destroy semantic structure and reading order. https://www.chhs.colostate.edu/accessibility/best-practices-how-tos/pdf-converted/ and conversion-tool comparisons noting preserved vs reflowable trade-offs.

2.4.4.platform: Disclosure / 'Show more' / 'Read more' (CMS content blocks, FAQ widgets)
2.4.4.name: Disclosure trigger with generic name and no expanded state
2.4.4.description: A 'Read more' / 'Show more' control expands hidden text but is a link or div with no aria-expanded and no aria-controls, and its accessible name is just the repeated generic phrase. Screen reader users get a list of identical 'Read more' controls with no context of what each reveals and no indication of open/closed state.
2.4.4.typicalMarkup:
Read more
Full product description...
2.4.4.whyAutoToolsMiss: axe can flag missing discernible text but cannot flag a NON-descriptive name that is technically present ('Read more' is a valid accessible name). Judging that 'Read more' is ambiguous out of context (2.4.4) and that the missing aria-expanded matters because this is a disclosure both require human semantic interpretation of purpose; the toggle role itself is not declared so no state rule fires.
2.4.4.realWorldNote: The APG disclosure pattern requires aria-expanded on the trigger; WebAIM and link-purpose guidance repeatedly cite generic repeated 'Read more'/'Learn more' from CMS widgets as a classic 2.4.4 ambiguous-link-text failure. https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/disclosure/

2.4.4.platform: WebAIM Million corpus (all builders) — buttons styled as div/span, icon-only controls
2.4.4.name: Empty button / icon control with no accessible name
2.4.4.description: A control is rendered as <div>, <span>, <a>, or an icon font/SVG with no text node and no aria-label, so its accessible name is empty. Screen readers announce 'button' or 'link' with nothing else. Common with hamburger menus, cart/search icons, social-share icons, and 'X' close buttons in page-builder widgets.
2.4.4.whyAutoToolsMiss: This one IS reliably caught by axe/WAVE ('button-name', 'link-name', 'Empty Button', 'Empty Link') — it is a pure programmatic check for an empty accessible name. Included for completeness as a high-prevalence baseline. Flagged humanJudgmentNeeded=false.
2.4.4.realWorldNote: WebAIM Million 2026: empty buttons on 30.6% of home pages, empty links on 46.3% — both in the top six errors: https://webaim.org/projects/million/

2.4.4.platform: CMS feed/listing widgets — WordPress 'Recent Posts', Shopify collection cards, Squarespace summary blocks
2.4.4.name: Repeated 'Read more' / 'Learn more' links with no in-context distinction
2.4.4.description: A looping CMS template emits the same link text ('Read more', 'Learn more', 'Shop now', 'View') for every card. A linter sees descriptive-enough text and a valid href, but a screen-reader user navigating by link list hears 'Read more, Read more, Read more' with no way to tell the destinations apart. The distinguishing context is only in an adjacent heading the link does not reference.
2.4.4.typicalMarkup:
Spring Collection

...

Read more

Gift Guide

...

Read more
2.4.4.whyAutoToolsMiss: 'Read more' is on some tools' generic-phrase blocklists, but many CMS templates use slightly varied phrasing or rely on the (technically present) heading nearby, so automated checks pass or only weakly flag. Judging whether the link purpose is clear FROM ITS CONTEXT — and whether the programmatic association (aria-labelledby to the heading) actually exists — needs a human reading the rendered page.

2.4.4.platform: Icon-only controls (font-icon or SVG) labelled only via the HTML title attribute (e.g. linked social icons, table action icons)
2.4.4.name: title attribute as the sole accessible name
2.4.4.description: A linked icon or icon button has no text and no aria-label; its only name is a title attribute. title is exposed inconsistently across screen readers (JAWS/NVDA/VoiceOver differ, and it is suppressed when an img alt is present), so the control is effectively unnamed for many users and provides only a flaky mouse-hover tooltip with no keyboard equivalent.
2.4.4.whyAutoToolsMiss: Per the accname algorithm title IS a valid (last-resort) name source, so axe computes a non-empty accessible name and passes the element. Whether the title is actually announced (and is adequate) depends on the screen reader and on whether better naming was intended; judging the real-world failure needs a human testing with AT.
2.4.4.realWorldNote: 24a11y 'Trials and Tribulations of the Title Attribute'; Silktide 'I thought title text improved accessibility. I was wrong.'; W3C issue 867 on title as sole accName. https://www.24a11y.com/2017/the-trials-and-tribulations-of-the-title-attribute/

2.4.4.platform: Generic / vague link and button text emitted by CMS widgets and listing components ('Read more', 'Learn more', 'Click here', arrow glyphs, repeated per card)
2.4.4.name: non-descriptive link/button text repeated out of context
2.4.4.description: A grid of cards or a blog listing renders many identical 'Read more' / 'Learn more' links with no aria-label disambiguation and no surrounding programmatic context. A screen-reader user pulling up a links list hears 'Learn more, Learn more, Learn more' with no way to tell destinations apart.
2.4.4.whyAutoToolsMiss: The links have non-empty accessible names, so name-presence checks pass. axe can flag identical link text going to different URLs in some configs, but judging whether 'Learn more' is sufficiently descriptive in context (and whether the heading association rescues it) is a semantic call about link purpose that needs a human.
2.4.4.realWorldNote: WCAG 2.4.4 Link Purpose; Deque/WebAIM and Silktide repeatedly cite CMS 'Read more'/'Learn more' widgets as a top real-world failure. https://www.deque.com/blog/text-links-practices-screen-readers/

2.4.4.platform: Theme components using icon fonts / inline SVG (Font Awesome, Bootstrap icons, Shopify Dawn header)
2.4.4.name: Icon-only button/link with no accessible name
2.4.4.description: A hamburger, search magnifier, close X, cart, or social-share control is rendered as a button/anchor whose only content is an <i> icon-font glyph or a decorative <svg> with no aria-label, no visually hidden text, and no title. Screen readers announce a bare "button" or "link" with no indication of what it does; voice-control users have nothing to target.
2.4.4.whyAutoToolsMiss: This one is largely catchable: axe/Lighthouse flag buttons and links with no accessible name. (Edge cases where an icon font ligature renders visible text the AT can read, or where a name exists but is wrong, still need human review, but the bare unnamed-control case is a reliable linter hit.)
2.4.4.realWorldNote: Icon-only controls are the canonical 4.1.2 "button with no accessible name" failure; Font Awesome's own docs and Shopify Dawn audits call it out. https://docs.fontawesome.com/web/dig-deeper/accessibility and https://testparty.ai/blog/shopify-dawn-theme-accessibility

2.4.4.platform: CMS list/grid widgets (WordPress blog loops, news cards, "recent posts")
2.4.4.name: Repeated "Read more" / "Learn more" links with no distinguishing purpose
2.4.4.description: A loop of post/product cards renders an identical generic call-to-action link under each item. When a screen-reader user pulls up the links list (or tabs through), they hear "Read more, link" / "Learn more, link" a dozen times with nothing to differentiate destinations. The descriptive context (the card heading) is programmatically separate from the link, so out of context the purpose is undeterminable.
2.4.4.typicalMarkup:
Spring Sale Tips

...

Read more

New Store Hours

...

Read more
2.4.4.whyAutoToolsMiss: Each link has non-empty text, so it passes the "link must have text" rule. Some tools heuristically flag the literal strings "read more"/"click here", but they cannot judge whether programmatically-determined context (an ancestor heading, aria-describedby) makes the purpose clear, nor whether the destinations actually differ — that needs reading the page.
2.4.4.realWorldNote: Ambiguous "Read more"/"Learn more" link soup from CMS content is a textbook 2.4.4 failure. https://www.visionaustralia.org/business-consulting/digital-access/blog/how-to-make-read-more-links-accessible and https://theadminbar.com/accessibility-weekly/ambiguous-links/

2.4.6.platform: Marketing/long-form pages built in Elementor, Divi, Wix, Webflow visual editors
2.4.6.name: Heading levels chosen for visual size, not document structure
2.4.6.description:
Authors pick heading tags by how big the text looks, producing skipped levels (h1 then h4), multiple or zero h1s, or styled
/

that look like headings but carry no heading role. The visual hierarchy and the programmatic outline diverge, breaking screen-reader heading navigation.
2.4.6.whyAutoToolsMiss:
Skipped heading levels are partially flagged ('heading-order'), but tools cannot detect a visually-styled

that SHOULD be a heading (no role to test against), nor judge whether the heading TEXT accurately describes its section (2.4.6). Matching the visual outline to the intended structure is a human reading/visual task.
2.4.6.realWorldNote: Elementor/Divi heading-misuse is a top page-builder audit finding: https://www.abrightclearweb.com/elementor-accessibility/ ; WebAIM Million also notes heading issues among manual-skewed problems.

2.4.6.platform: Hand-coded / framework icon buttons with aria-label overriding visible text (e.g. Bootstrap/Tailwind 'Submit' button decorated with aria-label="Send form now")
2.4.6.name: aria-label contradicts visible button text (Label in Name break)
2.4.6.description: A control has visible text but aria-label replaces it with different wording, so the accessible name no longer contains the visible label. Speech-input users cannot activate it by speaking the visible word, and screen-reader users hear different text than sighted users see. The classic W3C example is a 'Go' button whose aria-label is 'Find in this site'.
2.4.6.typicalMarkup: Cart (3)
2.4.6.whyAutoToolsMiss: axe/Lighthouse see a non-empty accessible name and a button with a role, so they pass it. They do not (reliably) compare the visible text node against the computed accessible name to detect that the visible label is absent from the name; deciding whether the visible word is 'contained' requires reading both strings and judging semantic equivalence.
2.4.6.realWorldNote: W3C WCAG failure F96 (accessible name not containing visible label text) uses the 'Go' button with aria-label 'Find in this site'; documented by Adrian Roselli and Ashlee Boyer ('Don't Overwrite Visual Labels With aria-label'). https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Techniques/failures/F96

2.4.6.platform: TinyMCE / CKEditor rich-text output embedded in any CMS (WordPress, Drupal, OJS)
2.4.6.name: Fake headings: bold/large paragraph instead of <h2>
2.4.6.description:

2.4.10.name: Heading levels chosen for visual size, not document structure
2.4.10.description:

/

3.3.1.platform: Toast / snackbar (MUI Snackbar misused, hand-rolled notifications, Toastify)
3.3.1.name: Toast rendered into a plain div, not a live region
3.3.1.description: A 'Saved!' or 'Error: try again' toast is injected into a positioned <div> with no role="status"/role="alert" and no aria-live. The message animates in visually but is never announced, so screen reader users never learn the action succeeded or failed.

Whether the absence of aria-live constitutes a violation depends on the div being a dynamically-injected status message, which a static scan of the final DOM cannot infer; you must observe that new content appeared without an announcement, a runtime + semantic judgment.

3.3.1.platform: MUI Snackbar, react-hot-toast, Bootstrap toasts, Shopify/WordPress 'added to cart' confirmations
3.3.1.name: Toast / status confirmation not in a live region
3.3.1.description: A success/error toast or 'Added to cart' / 'Form submitted' confirmation appears visually but is injected into a plain <div> with no role=status/alert and no aria-live, so screen readers announce nothing. 3.3.1.platform: Contact/checkout forms in Gravity Forms, Wix Forms, Shopify checkout, HubSpot forms
3.3.1.name: Required state and errors conveyed by color/asterisk only, not programmatically
3.3.1.description: Required fields are marked with a red asterisk or red border (color/symbol only) with no required/aria-required and no legend explaining the asterisk. On submit, errors are shown as red text near fields but not associated via aria-describedby and the field gets no aria-invalid, so screen readers never learn the field is required, that it errored, or what the message says.

3.3.1.platform: Required fields and inline validation in form builders / SPA forms where required and error state are visual-only (red border, red asterisk) without aria-required / aria-invalid / aria-describedby
3.3.1.name: form error and required state not programmatically associated
3.3.1.description: A field is marked required with a red asterisk and, on submit, an error appears as red text below it — but the input has no aria-required, no aria-invalid="true", and the error message is not tied via aria-describedby. Screen-reader users do not learn the field is required, that it errored, or what the suggested fix is.
3.3.1.typicalMarkup: Enter a valid email
3.3.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: The error markup is valid HTML and the field has a label, so structural scans pass. 3.3.1.platform: Multilingual sites / auto-translate widgets (Weglot, WPML, Google Website Translator)
3.3.1.name: Foreign-language passage with no lang, or stale html lang after translation
3.3.1.description: A page in one primary language embeds quotes, names, product blurbs, or whole machine-translated sections in another language without a lang attribute on those parts; or a translation layer swaps visible text but leaves <html lang="en"> unchanged. The screen reader reads French/Arabic/Japanese text with English phonetics (or vice versa), producing gibberish pronunciation. Often the page title/nav stays untranslated while the body is translated.
3.3.1.typicalMarkup: Our motto: Liberté, égalité, fraternité
3.3.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: Tools verify that an html lang exists and that lang values are valid BCP-47 tags, but they cannot read the text and detect that a passage is in a different language than its declared lang, nor that the declared page language no longer matches the rendered (translated) content. That requires language identification of the visible text.
3.3.1.realWorldNote: Missing lang on parts / mismatched page lang causes screen readers to mispronounce; documented for multilingual sites. https://benmyers.dev/blog/multilingual-web-accessibility/ and https://www.w3.org/TR/UNDERSTANDING-WCAG20/meaning-other-lang-id.html

3.3.2.platform: Radio group (custom styled radios, form-builder widgets, Shoelace-style components)
3.3.2.name: Custom radios: no grouping, every radio a tab stop, no arrow selection

3.3.2.name: placeholder used as the only label / instruction
